Memory Jogger.new: In the Pentagon Papers Case, the Nixon Administration sought to stop the \textit{New York Times} and \textit{Washington Post} from publishing a classified Vietnam War study; a 6--3 \textit{per curiam} held that the Government had not carried the ``heavy burden'' required to justify a prior restraint, with nine Justices writing separately (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/403/713/}{Justia}).

Judicial Votes.new: By a \textbf{6--3} vote, the Supreme Court \textbf{reversed} the Second Circuit (\textit{New York Times}) with directions to affirm the District Court, \textbf{affirmed} the D.C.\ Circuit (\textit{Washington Post}), and vacated all stays. The cases were argued June 26, 1971, and decided June 30, 1971 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/403/713/}{Justia}):

Analysis of Opinions.new: \item \textbf{Gag Orders on Trial Coverage:} The Court applied the same high barrier when

Analysis of Opinions.src: invalidating gag orders on media reporting of criminal trials in \textit{Nebraska Press Ass'n v.\ Stuart}, 427 U.S.\ 539 (1976)

In \textit{Snepp v.\ United States}, 444 U.S.\ 507 (1980), the Court enforced a former CIA agent's contractual prepublication review agreement and imposed a constructive trust on book royalties, distinguishing government employees with fiduciary access to secrets from outside newspapers.

Similarly, in \textit{Seattle Times Co.\ v.\ Rhinehart}, 467 U.S.\ 20 (1984), a unanimous Court held that a protective order barring a newspaper-litigant from publishing information obtained solely through compelled civil pretrial discovery is not a ``classic prior restraint'' triggering \textit{New York Times}'s heavy presumption.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Injunction Barred): Leaked Memo Exposing Official Deception.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: An anonymous Defense Department contractor leaks two classified documents to the \textit{National Ledger}: (1) a 2022 internal policy memo revealing that senior officials knowingly exaggerated intelligence estimates to justify a foreign cyber-operation; and (2) live cryptographic keys and exact GPS coordinates for an active U.S.\ naval convoy currently transiting a hostile strait. The Attorney General seeks an emergency federal court injunction barring publication of both documents, relying solely on the President's Article II Commander-in-Chief authority without pointing to any statute authorizing civil injunctions.

Under \textit{New York Times}, an injunction against \textbf{Document 1} is plainly unconstitutional under all six concurrences: it is historical policy criticism exposing official deception, posing no direct, immediate, and irreparable catastrophe.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Injunction Barred): A State's Leaked Emergency Plan.} A newspaper obtains a leaked copy of a State's confidential hurricane-evacuation plan, which shows that officials knew the plan's shelter capacity was badly inadequate. The Governor asks a federal court to enjoin publication, arguing that disclosure could cause public panic and help criminals predict where police will be deployed during a storm. Those predicted harms are speculative and depend on the reactions of third parties. Under the \textit{per curiam}, the restraint comes to court with a ``heavy presumption against its constitutional validity,'' and the Governor's ``surmise or conjecture'' (in Justice Brennan's phrase) about possible harm falls far short of Justice Stewart's showing of direct, immediate, and irreparable damage. The injunction must be denied (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/403/713/}{Justia}).
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Narrow Injunction Likely Upheld): Live Convoy Coordinates and Cryptographic Keys.} Same facts, as to Document 2.

Examples: Future Applications.src: \textbf{Document 2} squarely tests the \textit{Near}/\textit{New York Times} fault lines: under Justices Black and Douglas (absolutism) and Justice Marshall (lack of statutory authorization under \textit{Youngstown}), an injunction still fails; however, under Justice Brennan's ``transport already at sea'' exception and Justice Stewart's ``direct, immediate, and irreparable damage'' standard (joined by the three dissenters' deference framework), a majority of the Court's doctrinal spectrum would likely uphold a narrow injunction as to the live convoy coordinates and active cryptographic keys---and under Justice White's concurrence, publishing the cryptographic keys would also expose the paper to post-publication criminal prosecution under 18 U.S.C.\ \S~798.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Restraint Permitted): A Former Analyst's Memoir.} A former intelligence analyst signed an employment agreement promising to submit any writing about her work for prepublication review. She completes a memoir describing classified operations and announces that she will publish it without review. The Government sues to enjoin publication of the unreviewed manuscript and to impose a constructive trust on any profits. \textit{New York Times} does not control, because the analyst is not an outside newspaper publishing what it received; she voluntarily assumed a duty of confidentiality as a condition of access to secrets. Under \textit{Snepp v.\ United States}, 444 U.S. 507 (1980), the agreement is enforceable, and the Government may require review before publication and recover her profits if she breaches it.

\item \textbf{Fence-Sitter (Statutory Authorization): A Narrow Congressional Injunction Statute.} Congress enacts a statute authorizing federal courts, after an \textit{in camera} hearing, to enjoin publication of the names of covert intelligence officers currently serving abroad when publication would create a substantial risk of physical harm to them. A news site announces that it will publish a list of such names it has obtained. The statute answers the objection pressed by Justices White and Marshall, who stressed the absence of congressional authorization, and naming a deployed officer may resemble Brennan's troop-ship example. But Justices Black and Douglas would bar any prior restraint, and Stewart's standard demands that harm be direct, immediate, and irreparable, not merely a risk. Because \textit{New York Times} produced no majority rationale, whether such a statute could be applied to a publisher is unresolved.
